title: Building Judgment
coreMove: Strip identity and desire away from a decision until the basic reality can be seen and reasoned from.
sourcePressure: The source defines judgment as wisdom applied to external problems and says direction matters more than force when leverage is high. It emphasizes clear thinking from basics, empty calendar space, public honesty, identity shedding, mental models, inversion, falsifiability, and reading to rederive rather than memorize.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The wrong version praises intelligence, models, and contrarian opinions as status markers. This chapter must teach the reader to remove ego and desire from a decision so the facts become usable.

hook: a smart executive winning an argument in a conference room
a person deleting meetings from a calendar as productivity advice
counterintuition: being smart is less important than being wise
tryThisNow: write the opposite of your opinion
block thinking time on your calendar

exampleSpecs.domain: hospital transplant allocation review where a surgeon wants his own patient moved up the list
exampleSpecs.audience: a review chair who respects the surgeon but must separate advocacy from truth
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether scarce organ access is distorted by a persuasive identity and personal attachment
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the chair covers the patient names, reads only the lab values and time-on-list, and asks the surgeon to argue from the anonymized criteria before emotion reenters the room
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Two sealed transplant files sit under a transparent plastic name cover.

exampleSpecs.domain: wildfire incident commander deciding whether to defend a beloved historic lodge
exampleSpecs.audience: a commander whose crew has emotional ties to the town landmark
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether identity and nostalgia pull firefighters into a bad wind pattern
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she turns the lodge photo face down, traces the wind shift and escape route on the topo sheet, and cancels the defense because the map no longer supports the story
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A laminated topo sheet curls at the edge under a strip of ash.

exampleSpecs.domain: museum acquisitions team evaluating a donor's forged-looking manuscript
exampleSpecs.audience: a curator tempted by prestige and donor pressure
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the museum buys status and ignores provenance gaps
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the curator reads the provenance chain backward from the newest receipt, circles the first unverifiable owner, and removes the donor's name from the scoring sheet
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A brittle receipt is clipped to a manuscript sleeve with blue conservation tape.

exampleSpecs.domain: semiconductor yield engineer checking whether a favored process change actually improved output
exampleSpecs.audience: an engineer whose reputation is attached to the new etch recipe
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether a factory keeps amplifying a noisy improvement across millions of wafers
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: before seeing the latest batch label, he writes the falsifiable yield prediction, opens the blind wafer map, and accepts that the pattern is random clusters rather than his recipe working
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A wafer map glows with scattered red die failures on a dark inspection screen.

exampleSpecs.domain: public defender deciding whether a plea deal feels safe because it avoids trial or because it is actually just
exampleSpecs.audience: a lawyer under docket pressure who wants relief from uncertainty
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether a client accepts a life-altering plea because the attorney's anxiety masquerades as judgment
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she writes two columns labeled client facts and my relief, moves every sentence about docket pressure out of the recommendation, and rereads the evidence timeline alone
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A plea offer rests beside a courthouse vending-machine receipt.

exampleSpecs.domain: archaeological field lead deciding whether a rare shard supports the team's pet migration theory
exampleSpecs.audience: a researcher whose grant narrative depends on a clean story
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether desire for an elegant finding overrides a messy excavation layer
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: before announcing the find, he places the shard back beside the soil-depth tags, notices the mixed layer, and rewrites the field note from discovery to contamination risk
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A painted ceramic shard rests beside three soil-depth tags in a shallow tray.

skillTargets: separate desire for an outcome from evidence about the outcome
choose a falsifiable test over a comforting explanation
recognize identity-protective reasoning in high-stakes decisions
apply inversion and base principles to an ambiguous choice
evaluate when empty space for thinking is decision infrastructure rather than leisure

tryThisNowSpec: Take one decision you want to go a certain way. Write the sentence you most hope is true, then write what would prove it false if you had no name, pride, money, or tribe attached to the answer.

sourceAnchors.name: Richard Feynman
sourceAnchors.detail: the source points to Six Easy Pieces as an example of building mathematics from counting through an unbroken chain of logic without hiding behind definitions
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Feynman makes clear thinking look almost plain: start with the number line and keep every step visible.

sourceAnchors.name: Warren Buffett
sourceAnchors.detail: the source cites Buffett’s rule to praise specifically and criticize generally as part of radical honesty without needless personal attack
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Buffett’s rule keeps honesty aimed at reality instead of turning it into a private weapon.

sourceAnchors.name: Nassim Taleb
sourceAnchors.detail: the source names Taleb in connection with black swans and tail events as mental models for extreme probabilities
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Taleb’s black swan frame matters when the average case is the wrong place to look.

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: prevents the timestamp+named-protagonist template from dominating the chapter

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm — a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following 'concrete anchor -> abstract rule -> elaboration'
